title: Tanishk Bagchi Says He Earned 'Zero' From Saiyaara Title Track as YRF Royalty Dispute Goes Public
excerpt: The composer claims Rs 8 lakh in royalties remains unpaid despite the song’s massive streaming success, reigniting debate over how Indian music labels compensate creators.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Tanishk Bagchi claims he earned 'zero' from the Saiyaara title track after production costs.
  • He alleges Rs 8 lakh in unpaid royalties despite the song's streaming success.
  • YRF asserts all payments were made as per contract, sharing royalties among three composers.
  • The dispute highlights systemic issues in how Indian music compensates creators.
  • Bagchi's complaint pressures YRF to improve transparency in royalty accounting.

Tanishk Bagchi's Instagram statement
  • Composer Tanishk Bagchi alleged on Instagram that he earned “zero” from the Saiyaara title track after production costs consumed his entire fee from Yash Raj Films.
  • Bagchi claims Rs 8 lakh in royalties remains unpaid despite the song generating millions of streams and views across platforms.
  • YRF responded saying all dues were paid “as per contract” and that royalties are shared equally among the song’s three composers.
  • The dispute highlights a broader structural problem in Indian music where composers receive one-time payments rather than sustained royalty income.

The Complaint

Music composer Tanishk Bagchi took to Instagram on July 18 with a detailed public statement alleging that he earned nothing from the title track of Saiyaara, one of the biggest Hindi film soundtracks in recent years. The 2025 romantic drama directed by Mohit Suri became one of the highest-grossing Indian romantic films, and its title track emerged as a streaming juggernaut.

Bagchi wrote that the experience marked his first collaboration with YRF Entertainment and that he had “agreed to everything because I believed in the music.” He described investing extensive personal effort in the production, composition, vocal tuning, arrangements, and mixing.

“Whatever YRF had paid me, all of that nominal amount was used to do the live and mixes,” Bagchi wrote. “What was left was zero. Yes, that’s what I earned from a song so big.”

The composer added that according to his royalty statement, Rs 8 lakh — roughly $9,500 — remains unpaid. He described the amount as inadequate given the song’s commercial reach.

“I’m not writing this for sympathy. I’m writing this because I know what I put into this song, and I know the sacrifices I made to bring it to life.”

— Tanishk Bagchi, composer

YRF’s Response

Yash Raj Films issued a formal clarification within hours, stating that “every collaborator” had been paid according to contractual terms. A YRF spokesperson noted that the Saiyaara title track was a collaboration between three composers — Tanishk Bagchi, Faheem Abdullah, and Arslan Nizami — and that royalties are shared equally among all three as contractually agreed.

“We are deeply thankful for their brilliance in creating a timeless song that has touched a million hearts,” the statement read. “Royalties for the title track have been shared and will continue to be shared by YRF equally between all three composers.”

The studio’s statement did not directly address Bagchi’s claim that his production costs consumed the entire upfront payment, nor did it specify the total royalty pool or the timeline for pending payments.

A Systemic Problem

Bagchi has previously spoken about the “unfair” realities of royalty structures in the Indian music industry. Despite commanding billions of views across streaming platforms, Indian composers and musicians often receive one-time payments rather than sustained income proportional to a song’s commercial performance.

The dispute highlights a persistent tension between India’s booming music streaming market and the compensation structures that predate the digital era. India’s music streaming industry has grown rapidly, with platforms like Spotify, JioSaavn, and YouTube Music driving massive consumption numbers. But the royalty frameworks governing how that revenue flows back to creators remain opaque and, according to many artists, inadequate.

The emergence of AI-generated recreations of hit songs — including versions of Saiyaara rendered in the late Kishore Kumar’s voice that have racked up millions of views on YouTube — has added another dimension to the compensation problem, diverting legitimate streaming revenue while original artists remain undercompensated.

What’s Next

The public nature of Bagchi’s complaint puts pressure on YRF and other major labels to increase transparency around royalty accounting. For the broader Indian music ecosystem, the dispute underscores the need for updated contractual standards that reflect the economics of streaming-era distribution.
